metadata.name: Acute pharyngitis (sore throat)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine — mostly viral; exclude serious causes (epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess)

overview.short_description: Acute inflammation of the pharynx causing sore throat, usually viral and self-limiting, requiring assessment to identify the minority needing antibiotics (streptococcal) or urgent care (airway/deep-space infection).
overview.detailed_description: Sore throat is a very common presentation. Most cases are viral and resolve within a week. The main tasks are to use clinical scoring (Centor/McIsaac or FeverPAIN) to estimate streptococcal probability and antibiotic need, avoid unnecessary antibiotics, and recognise red flags for airway compromise or deep-space infection.
overview.pathophysiology: Viral or bacterial infection causes mucosal inflammation of the pharynx and tonsils, producing pain, erythema and sometimes exudate, with local lymphoid reaction (tender cervical nodes).
overview.etiology: Mostly viruses (rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronavirus, influenza, EBV). Bacterial: group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus (GAS) most important; less often other bacteria. Consider EBV (glandular fever) in young adults.
overview.natural_history: Most resolve within ~1 week regardless of cause; antibiotics only modestly shorten streptococcal illness and reduce complications.
overview.prognosis: Excellent; suppurative (peritonsillar abscess) and non-suppurative (rheumatic fever, rare in high-income settings) complications are uncommon.

prevalence.value: Among the most common reasons for primary-care visits, especially in children/young adults.

incidence.value: Very common year-round, peaking in winter.

mortality.value: Negligible; serious outcomes only via rare airway/deep-space infection or rheumatic complications.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; streptococcal more common in children 5-15 years.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; rheumatic fever risk higher in some low-resource settings.

risk_factors.pregnancy: Not a risk factor; affects medication choice.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Recurrent tonsillitis; consider immunodeficiency if very frequent/severe.

symptoms.importance: Their PRESENCE argues AGAINST streptococcal cause (favours viral)

symptoms.symptom: Tender, enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

symptoms.importance: Scoring feature; also seen in EBV

negative_findings.finding: Presence of cough/coryza (i.e., typical viral features)
negative_findings.why_important: Makes streptococcal infection less likely (lowers Centor score) — supports avoiding antibiotics

negative_findings.finding: No trismus, no muffled 'hot potato' voice, no drooling, no stridor
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues against peritonsillar abscess and airway emergencies

history_questions.question: Do you have a cough, runny nose, and hoarseness?
How high is the fever and how rapidly did it start?
Any difficulty opening the mouth, drooling, muffled voice, or difficulty breathing?
Young adult with prolonged sore throat, marked fatigue, and swollen glands?
Recent antibiotics or immunosuppression?
history_questions.why_ask: Risk/atypical presentations; agranulocytosis if on certain drugs

physical_examination.expected_finding: Erythema +/- exudate; asymmetry/bulging suggests peritonsillar abscess

physical_examination.examination: Airway signs (voice, drooling, trismus, stridor); posterior pharynx/epiglottis caution

physical_examination.expected_finding: May be enlarged in glandular fever

laboratory_tests.test_name: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) / throat culture for GAS
laboratory_tests.indication: When streptococcal infection is likely by score and confirmation changes management (varies by local guidance)
Suspected glandular fever (young adult, prolonged symptoms, lymphadenopathy)

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Laryngoscopy by ENT if epiglottitis/airway concern (in a controlled setting)
other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Throat swab for GAS as above

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical diagnosis of acute sore throat; use a scoring tool to estimate streptococcal probability and guide antibiotics. Centor (fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, ABSENCE of cough) and McIsaac add age adjustment; FeverPAIN (Fever, Purulence, Attend rapidly <=3 days, Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza).

diagnostic_scores.value: FeverPAIN 0-1 or Centor 0-2 -> low strep probability, no antibiotics; FeverPAIN 4-5 or Centor 3-4 -> higher probability, consider antibiotics/testing.

cutoff_values.value: Centor >=3 and FeverPAIN >=4 indicate higher streptococcal likelihood (NICE NG84).

differential_diagnosis.differences: Higher fever, exudate, tender nodes, NO cough; higher score
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have a cough? (absence favours strep)

differential_diagnosis.differences: Young adult, prolonged, marked fatigue, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Splenic rupture (avoid contact sports), airway obstruction
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you very tired with swollen glands lasting more than a week?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Unilateral severe pain, trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the pain one-sided with difficulty opening your mouth?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Rapid, toxic, drooling, stridor, tripod posture, minimal oral findings
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_exam: Distressed, stridor; do NOT examine throat aggressively
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_imaging: Lateral neck X-ray in stable cases (thumbprint sign)
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any drooling, muffled voice, or difficulty breathing?

differential_diagnosis.differences: On causative drug (e.g., carbimazole, clozapine), unwell, may have mouth ulcers
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_symptoms: Sore throat + fever on relevant medication
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are you on medicines like carbimazole or clozapine?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a cough and runny nose along with the sore throat?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Cough present -> lower strep likelihood, avoid antibiotics

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the pain one-sided with trismus/muffled voice/drooling or any breathing difficulty?

next_best_question.current_situation: Acute sore throat, no airway red flags
next_best_question.question: Do you have a cough/cold symptoms, and how high is your fever?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Viral features/low score -> reassure, no antibiotics; high score -> consider testing/antibiotics; airway red flags -> emergency referral

next_best_test.why: Estimates streptococcal probability to guide antibiotics
Confirm strep in higher-score cases where it changes management

red_flags.finding: Stridor, drooling, difficulty breathing, or inability to swallow saliva
red_flags.immediate_action: Airway emergency — do not examine throat aggressively; urgent ENT/anaesthetics (suspect epiglottitis)

red_flags.finding: Unilateral severe pain with trismus, muffled voice, uvular deviation
Severe sore throat with fever in a patient on carbimazole/clozapine or immunosuppressed
Dehydration/inability to maintain oral intake, or systemically very unwell

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected peritonsillar abscess or deep-space infection; recurrent severe tonsillitis for ENT assessment (tonsillectomy criteria).
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent documented tonsillitis meeting surgical criteria; persistent unexplained sore throat (exclude malignancy in smokers/older adults).
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Airway compromise (epiglottitis), inability to swallow saliva, or neutropenic sepsis.

late: Post-streptococcal: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis (rare in high-income settings)

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance (most viral, resolve in ~1 week); adequate fluids and rest.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; Ibuprofen/NSAID; Phenoxymethylpenicillin; Macrolide. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: NICE_NG84.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Fluids, rest, warm/soothing drinks; avoid smoking.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net for airway/deep-space signs or no improvement in ~1 week.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Analgesia/antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen), medicated lozenges/anaesthetic sprays for symptom relief. ANTIBIOTICS ONLY for higher-probability streptococcal cases (high Centor/FeverPAIN) or systemically unwell — first-line phenoxymethylpenicillin (avoid amoxicillin if EBV possible due to rash; use a macrolide if penicillin-allergic). Consider delayed prescribing strategies (NICE NG84).

patient_education.home_advice: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and get better within a week without antibiotics. Painkillers, lozenges, and plenty of fluids help. Get urgent help if you have trouble breathing or swallowing your own saliva, drooling, a muffled voice, or one-sided severe throat pain with difficulty opening your mouth.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: معظم حالات التهاب الحلق سببها فيروسات وتتحسّن خلال أسبوع دون مضادات حيوية. تفيد مسكّنات الألم والأقراص المهدّئة وكثرة السوائل. اطلب المساعدة العاجلة إذا صعُب التنفّس أو بلع الريق، أو حدث سيلان اللعاب، أو تغيّر الصوت، أو ألم شديد في جانب واحد مع صعوبة فتح الفم.
patient_education.prevention: Hand hygiene, avoiding close contact when unwell.
patient_education.warning_signs: Difficulty breathing or swallowing saliva, drooling, muffled voice, one-sided severe pain with trismus, or symptoms lasting beyond a week.

prevention.vaccination: No specific vaccine (influenza vaccination reduces some viral cases).

evidence.evidence_level: High for scoring-guided antibiotic use and self-limiting viral course.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by NICE_NG84; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
